video_title: AI Could Change Markets Forever | Systematic Investor | Ep.417
gist: Rob Carver and his co-host survey a market they describe as 'teetering' — sovereign bond supply fears colliding with US Treasury buybacks, crude just under $100 with the SPR still draining, and trend followers up ~12% YTD but running well below average risk. Despite the AI-themed title, the AI discussion is a skeptical minority of the episode; the densest material is on the Simplify 'CTA' ETF's apparent style drift out of diversified managed futures into a long-only energy book, on what level to fit trading rules at (instrument vs asset class vs global), and on why high volatility is not uniformly good for trend following.

themes.theme: Sovereign Bond Supply vs. Treasury Buybacks

insights.claim: Norway's sovereign wealth fund has proposed cutting government debt from 70% to 50% of its bond portfolio, which at roughly 25% fixed income weighting is about a 5% shift of a $2 trillion-plus portfolio, or on the order of $100 billion of government bonds to be reallocated.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver and host (Niels)
insights.so_what: A single price-insensitive holder of that size stepping back from govvies is a structural supply/demand headwind for long-end sovereign yields and a potential source of the sustained bond trend CTAs have lacked.

insights.claim: US Treasury buyback operations announced under Bessent — an expansion of the long-end program on August 19 and a $6 billion operation in the 10-to-20-year sector — are described as trivially small relative to the size of the US bond market.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Treating buyback headlines as a yield backstop is a mistake at current scale; the trade is in the signaling, not the flow, unless the size rises by orders of magnitude.
insights.quote: It's like a drop a drop inside a drop in the ocean.

insights.claim: The escalating size of Treasury buyback operations plus explicit references to the roughly $1 trillion sitting in the Treasury General Account suggests the buyback program may be the early stage of a much larger yield-management effort rather than a one-off.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Watch buyback operation sizes sequentially — an accelerating cadence would be an early tell that the Treasury is stepping in against the long end, which would cap a short-bond trend.

insights.claim: Rob Carver is currently positioned short US 10-year bonds and short Korean 10-year bonds in his own systematic portfolio.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A live disclosed position from a systematic trader showing that trend signals in global rates are currently pointing short, not just that the narrative is bearish.
insights.quote: Full disclosure, I am short um US bonds, specifically 10 years.

insights.claim: Bonds were the primary driver of CTA returns from late 2021 into early 2023 but have detracted over the last couple of years, so a renewed large bond trend would restore a return engine that trend followers have been missing.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Sector attribution matters: sustained rate trends disproportionately lift managed futures returns because fixed income is a large sleeve of the typical CTA portfolio.

themes.theme: CTA ETF Style Drift and Industry Structure

insights.claim: The Simplify managed futures strategy trading under the ticker CTA has reportedly removed its subadvisor, with the manager overriding the subadvisor's systematic signals to set exposure directly.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Holders using this ETF as a proxy for diversified managed futures exposure may no longer own what they underwrote; verify the mandate before relying on it as a portfolio diversifier.

insights.claim: According to the reporting discussed, the fund went from trading over 50 markets to holding essentially only energy positions with no short positions at all, which destroys the cross-market diversification that makes low-Sharpe trend strategies work.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A concentrated long-only energy book has a completely different correlation profile to equities than diversified trend, so its role in an allocator's portfolio changes entirely.

insights.claim: Rob Carver says that if he held the ETF as a proxy for CTA exposure he would sell it immediately because it no longer delivers that exposure, even though the intervention has performed well recently.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Good recent performance is not a reason to hold a product that has stopped doing the job it was bought for — the diversification role, not the return, is the investment case.
insights.quote: I would 100% sell it now because it no longer ticks that box.

insights.claim: ETF wrappers carry a governance weakness relative to manager-run funds: the underlying strategy can change and the sub-manager can be replaced with little or no advance notice, whereas institutional investors in traditional funds actively police style drift.
insights.speaker: host (Niels) and Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Structure risk belongs in ETF due diligence alongside fees and tracking — the cheapest wrapper can carry the weakest mandate protection.
insights.quote: it appears you can just one day wake up and say today I will no longer be um you know a managed futures ETF

insights.claim: Institutional investor aversion to style drift is so strong that it historically inhibited research and innovation inside large CTAs — Carver was hired at AHL to build a new strategy but could not obtain a meaningful allocation because investors only wanted diversified trend following.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Explains why innovation in managed futures tends to arrive in new vehicles rather than inside flagship funds — and why mandate purity is the product allocators are actually buying.

insights.claim: Millennium is reported to be nearing $100 billion in assets under management, raising capital seemingly at will while most managers struggle to raise anything.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Continued concentration of allocator capital into a few multi-strategy platforms squeezes capacity and talent pricing for everyone else in the systematic space.

themes.theme: Autumn 2026 Tape: Flat Risk, Waiting for a Catalyst

insights.claim: As of mid-September 2026 the BTOP50 index is up 1.15% in September and 12.42% year-to-date, the SG CTA index up 1.16% and 12.41%, the SG Trend index up just under 1% and 12.1%, and the short-term traders index up 12 basis points in September and 5.9% year-to-date at much lower volatility.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: A strong managed futures year in progress with tight dispersion between benchmarks — the average trend manager has already banked a double-digit return into a quiet September.

insights.claim: Traditional benchmarks show the MSCI World Index down 55 basis points in September but up 12.78% for the year, the world government bond index up 20 basis points in September and down 32 basis points for the year, and the S&P 500 total return index down 61 basis points in September and up 12.45% year-to-date.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: Trend following is matching equity returns year-to-date while global bonds are flat to negative — an unusually favorable relative setup for the managed futures allocation case.

insights.claim: Carver is running at roughly one third of his average risk, up about 7.5% on the year with most of that made in the first few weeks and flat since, concentrated in equities and energies alongside a short bond position.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A disciplined systematic book sitting at a third of normal risk is a quantitative read that trend signals across markets are weak and uncorroborated right now.

insights.claim: Markets feel poised on the edge of a regime break with widespread worry but no price reaction outside bonds, which is a qualitative read rather than a statistical one.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Low realized movement alongside high stated anxiety favors convexity — cheap optionality or trend exposure that pays if the break comes, rather than carry.
insights.quote: it does feel like one of those environments where the market's kind of tottering on the edge of something, right?

insights.claim: Crude oil has been hovering just below $100 despite a war running since the beginning of the year, while the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is still being drawn down every week at a slowing but non-zero pace toward a point where no further releases are possible.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: SPR exhaustion removes a persistent supply valve under the oil market and is a datable, watchable catalyst for an energy breakout above $100.

insights.claim: The candidate catalysts for breaking the current market stalemate are the US midterms, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve reaching the point where it can no longer be drawn down, and uncertainty around the new Fed chair who has declined to signal his policy intentions.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A concrete catalyst watchlist for timing the re-emergence of trends after a flat, low-risk period.

themes.theme: What Level to Fit Trading Rules At

insights.claim: Fitting forecast weights separately for every individual instrument produces mostly noise and not much signal, and is essentially overfitting with poor robustness.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A direct answer for DIY systematic traders: do not let per-market performance differences drive per-market rule weights.

insights.claim: Fitting rule weights by asset class and fitting them globally across all instruments both perform roughly equally well, so either is defensible provided the portfolio contains enough instruments.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Removes a long-running source of complexity debate — the choice between these two levels is not where returns are won or lost.

insights.claim: The most robust approach found is a meta-fit: run all three fitting levels — individual, asset class, and global — and allocate a third of risk capital to each, which is equivalent to averaging their outputs.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A generalizable ensemble principle: when you cannot determine which model specification is right, weight them equally rather than choosing.

insights.claim: Carver intends to move his own strategy to the averaged three-level fit even though he expects the resulting returns to correlate about 0.98 to 0.99 with his current approach, making it a low-priority change.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Calibrates expectations: methodological refinements at this level of a trend system produce marginal, not transformative, changes to the return stream.

insights.claim: A small portfolio — for example two bond markets, three equity markets, one FX and a couple of energy markets — should definitely not be fitted by asset class because there are not enough instruments to produce reasonable amounts of data.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: The right fitting level is a function of instrument count, so retail-scale systems should default to a single global fit.

insights.claim: The 'matrix fit' approach favored by quants from outside the CTA industry — which can allocate more to fast trend in equities purely because it diversifies and is cheap to trade there even if it loses money standalone — adds a lot of complexity without much value.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Warns allocators against equating methodological sophistication with edge when evaluating quant managers.

insights.claim: Carver's default stance is to do no fitting at all and to introduce fitting only where there is strong evidence it adds value, with any such fitting required to be robust and out of sample.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A prior-of-simplicity discipline that flips the burden of proof onto every added parameter in a system.
insights.quote: my prior is to do no fitting

themes.theme: Where Discretion Is Allowed in a Systematic Process

insights.claim: The claim circulating online that 'systematic trading does not mean blindly taking every setup' is a redefinition of the word — systematic trading literally means executing exactly what the system says, and the person making the claim conceded the point.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A due-diligence line for allocators: a manager who overrides signals at will has no testable track record, whatever they call themselves.
insights.quote: systematic trading does not mean blindly taking every setup

insights.claim: Having a trading system and feeling free to ignore it when it doesn't suit you is the worst way to combine discretion with systematic methods, primarily because it makes the backtest meaningless as evidence that the system works.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Discretionary overrides destroy the only evidence base an allocator has for the strategy, which is a valuation issue not just a philosophical one.

insights.claim: The correct way to combine discretion with systematic trading is to confine discretion entirely to the 'what should I buy and when' decision, while trading speed, position closing, position sizing, cost management and risk management are all handled by scientific rule-based processes.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A concrete architecture for hybrid discretionary/systematic funds and an audit checklist for allocators evaluating them.

insights.claim: If bad buy decisions were the only error retail traders made you would expect roughly half to make money since worst case they are coin-flipping, but the actual figure is around 95% losing and 5% making money, and worse for day traders — proving the losses come from position sizing, cost and risk management rather than entries.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Reframes where trading edge is actually lost, and is the empirical case for systematizing everything except entry selection.
insights.quote: 95% of retail traders lose money about 5% make money

insights.claim: Academic research on retail traders and on discretionary long-only institutional stock pickers found many mutual fund managers have genuine skill at finding good stocks but terrible skill at choosing when to exit them.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Entry skill and exit skill are separable, so manager evaluation should decompose attribution rather than judging overall returns.

insights.claim: Most modern trend models enter trends at broadly similar times, so the real differentiator between managers is how they manage risk during the trade and where they exit — that is where genuine skill shows up.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: When comparing CTAs, exit and risk-scaling methodology is the variable worth diligencing, not the entry signal.

insights.claim: The biggest live methodological debate in the trend industry is whether to volatility-scale positions after entry or to let a winning position grow as large as possible.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Vol-scaling policy drives the shape of a manager's return distribution and is a first-order question to ask any CTA.

insights.claim: Carver's new book, The Art and Science of Trading, is out on December 1 and is aimed at traders using non-leveraged instruments, where you cannot simply take every position you want and instead need to rank positions and apply path-dependent swap rules — which he argues makes running a portfolio without leverage more complicated in many ways.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
entities: The Art and Science of Trading
insights.so_what: The unleveraged portfolio construction problem — ranking and swapping rather than sizing freely — is an under-covered constraint for cash-account and retirement-account systematic investors.

themes.theme: AI in Quant Research and the Coming Retail AI Herd

insights.claim: The biggest risk of using AI in the quant research phase is that it will simply overfit, which requires wrapping it in strong guard rails of code not written by AI.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: AI-generated strategy research needs the same out-of-sample discipline as human research, only enforced mechanically — a governance gap in many new AI-driven funds.

insights.claim: In a real AI code review of Carver's research code, the AI found one serious bug and a couple of minor ones but simultaneously introduced a larger bug that would have deleted all short positions, leaving the strategy long-only.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A concrete failure mode showing AI code changes can silently alter a strategy's entire exposure profile — operational risk that would not surface until live P&L diverged.
insights.quote: all short positions would be deleted by a check the AI thought that should be in

insights.claim: Live production trading code written by AI with no or insufficient human oversight would be terrifying, and agentic setups where AI agents talk to other AI agents and write the code that way are the specific pattern that worries Carver most.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Operational-risk diligence on AI-enabled managers should focus on whether a human verifies every AI-written change, not on whether AI is used at all.

insights.claim: AI governance can borrow directly from investment risk management, because systematic managers already know that oversight, governance and processes around code implementation are key for anything trading automatically — AI does not change that approach and if anything strengthens the need for it.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Quant firms have a transferable governance advantage over generalist firms adopting AI, which may show up as fewer operational incidents.

insights.claim: AI models' consistently favorable verdicts on trend following are circular and carry no independent information value, because the models were trained on internet content written largely by trend following advocates and are simply reflecting that back.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Using LLM consensus as validation for an allocation thesis is measuring your own marketing, a trap for anyone polling AI on investment questions.
insights.quote: it's been trained on reading the internet

insights.claim: A wave of retail and institutional traders now trading on consumer-grade AI models could increase market turnover, risk and volatility, but it is too early to test empirically because not enough people are doing it yet.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Flags an emerging microstructure question — watch turnover and volatility metrics for the first empirical evidence of an AI-driven flow effect.

insights.claim: The AI trading wave may resemble the meme stock craze — markets get silly for a while and then partially normalize — but meme stock effects never fully went away, and AI could intensify them rather than replace them.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A historical template for sizing and timing the AI-retail distortion, with the caveat that the distortion may be persistent rather than a discrete episode.
insights.quote: I think personally think Tesla is the biggest meme stock in the world

insights.claim: The trade in a herd of uninformed AI-driven retail investors is to be on the other side of their trades — the poker-table logic of wanting opponents who have no idea what they are doing — though Carver admits he does not yet know how to capture it.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Points at mean-reversion and liquidity-provision strategies as the likely beneficiaries of an AI-retail flow wave, an opportunity set not yet formalized.
insights.quote: I think we're going to see a herd of uninformed AIdriven uh retail investors

insights.claim: An Alpha Architect post revisiting VIX-and-trend-following research a decade after the original work concludes the effect still seems to work, with the idea being that you should trade faster when market volatility is higher.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A vol-conditioned speed overlay has now survived ten years of out-of-sample data, which is rare for a published anomaly.

insights.claim: Carver's own strategy does the opposite in spirit — he trades less momentum when the market is more volatile — and notes that the finding that high volatility is bad for trend following is counterintuitive to investors who picture trend as a straddle payoff that profits from any large move.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Undermines the common 'long volatility' marketing framing of trend following and explains why CTAs can lose in high-VIX regimes.

insights.claim: High volatility means at least three structurally different things: a 2008-style secular turning point where markets fall and keep falling, a 2020 COVID-style wide V, and a 2025 tariff tantrum-style extremely narrow V — so broad-brush statements about volatility and trend are unsafe.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: A taxonomy that tells you which speed of trend system should work in a given drawdown, and explains dispersion between CTAs in the same stress event.
insights.quote: high volatility could mean one of three different things

insights.claim: In a V-shaped market you want to be either very slow or very fast but not medium — during the wider COVID V, fast trend worked because it could ride down and back up and very slow trend also did well, while medium speed did worst.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Speed diversification, not speed selection, is the robust response to not knowing the shape of the next drawdown.

insights.claim: The tariff tantrum V was so fast that fast trend following probably did worst of all because it was whipsawed, while medium and slow trend held through and did not do too badly — the reverse of the COVID ordering.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the 'speed up when vol rises' rule in the most recent stress event, so the overlay carries real regime risk.

insights.claim: The practical objection to speeding up in high volatility is that you cannot know in advance which type of volatility regime you are entering, so the overlay may be right on average and catastrophically wrong in a specific event.
insights.speaker: host (Niels)
insights.so_what: A generalizable test for any conditional overlay: does it require forecasting the regime, and what happens when you get the regime wrong?

insights.claim: Carver has a prior toward simplicity and says he will not be implementing the VIX-conditioned speed idea in his own portfolio, while still arguing it is not a random data-mining finding because it has a coherent story behind it.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Separates 'this result is real' from 'this belongs in my system' — the discipline that stops research consumption turning into strategy bloat.

insights.claim: A Man Group Insights article runs a rolling regression of manager returns on standard factors back to the early 2000s and finds meaningful variation in the R-squared over time, meaning the share of quant manager performance explained by common factors is not stable.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Factor-replication of quant equity managers works better in some periods than others, so fee-justification analyses are regime-dependent.

insights.claim: The quant winter of 2018 to 2020 was a period when classic factors such as value and momentum performed poorly, and it is the reference case for factor-driven drawdowns.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Any quant equity allocation should be stress-tested against a repeat of the 2018-2020 factor drawdown window.

insights.claim: Quant equity managers are not all the same and should not be assumed to be running the same basic factors underneath, and there appears to be an increasing amount of idiosyncratic performance and available diversification in quant equity over the last few years.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Rising idiosyncratic dispersion argues for allocating across multiple quant equity managers rather than treating the category as one factor bet.

insights.claim: Diversification across managers is the right default because it is very hard to pick which manager will be best, but diversification has a habit of disappearing precisely during events like the quant winter when everyone suffers together.
insights.speaker: Rob Carver
insights.so_what: Manager diversification is not a substitute for strategy-level diversification, since correlations converge in exactly the drawdowns it was meant to protect against.
insights.quote: diversification has a habit of going away during events like the quant winter
